justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three time horizons, starting near current market levels and gradually moving higher. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 11.27 is essentially anchored to the prevailing price or index level, with only minimal expected movement based on recent momentum and mean-reversion tendencies. The slight upward bias in the one-week estimate of 11.35 reflects a continuation of whatever near-term trend was present at forecast time, while the one-month estimate of 11.50 incorporates a longer-run drift assumption — likely based on historical average returns or a mild bullish tilt derived from fundamental or macro conditions at the time. None of these shifts are dramatic; they represent an expectation of slow, grinding appreciation rather than any sharp directional move.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval is relatively tight (10.90 to 11.65), which makes sense because short-horizon forecasts benefit from low volatility accumulation — prices simply don't move that much in a single session under normal conditions. By one week, the interval widens to 10.50–12.20, capturing several days of potential volatility, news flow, and momentum shifts. At one month, the interval stretches to 9.80–13.20, acknowledging that over four or more weeks, macro surprises, earnings, geopolitical events, and sentiment swings can push prices substantially in either direction. The width roughly scales with the square root of time, consistent with standard diffusion-based volatility modeling.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these wider intervals. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward aggressive tightening, or a sudden risk-off event such as a geopolitical escalation or financial stress episode could easily breach the lower bounds. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst — such as a surprise dovish pivot, better-than-expected earnings, or a resolution of an ongoing macro uncertainty — could push prices above the upper bounds. Liquidity conditions and broader market sentiment can also amplify moves in either direction more than historical volatility alone would suggest.

Finally, model uncertainty itself is a source of tail risk that my stated intervals may understate. The confidence intervals are derived from assumptions about volatility, drift, and distributional shape that may not hold during regime changes or black swan events. Fat-tailed distributions in financial returns mean that extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict.
